title: Maharaja Ranjit Singh
hook: he unites Punjab in 1799 and covers the Harmandir in gold, giving it the name the world knows

segments.voice: Yesterday, the misl, twelve Sikh confederacies. Your line was twelve, and one. Today, the young leader from one of those twelve who made them one kingdom. Day two hundred ninety-three.

Ask almost anyone to picture a Sikh place of worship, and they'll see the same thing. A shining building in the middle of a still pool, its upper walls and dome glowing gold, reflected upside down in the water. Photos of it are on kitchen walls and phone screens around the world. But for most of its history it didn't look like that. It was built of brick and stone. The gold came later, from a king. Today: Maharaja Ranjit Singh.
screen: `A SHINING BUILDING IN A STILL POOL.` → `ON WALLS AND PHONES WORLDWIDE.` → `THE GOLD CAME LATER.`

segments.voice: Ranjit Singh was born in 1780, the son of the leader of the Sukerchakia misl. As a small child he survived smallpox, which left him blind in one eye. He became chief as a boy, and at nineteen, in 1799, he rode into Lahore and took the city. Over the next years he brought the misls and much of the land around them under one rule. In 1801 he was proclaimed Maharaja, great king, of Punjab. He ruled for almost forty years, until his death in 1839. His was a Sikh kingdom, but not only for Sikhs. Muslims and Hindus served at the top of his government; his foreign minister was a Muslim scholar. Then there's the gold. Ranjit Singh gave generously to many places of worship, and above all to the Harmandir in Amritsar, the temple the Afghans had destroyed and the Sikhs had rebuilt. Over years of work, its upper stories were covered in gilded copper, and inlaid marble was added below. Visitors from Britain saw it shining and called it the Golden Temple. The name stuck, and the world has used it ever since. Sikhs usually call it Harmandir Sahib, the house of God, or Darbar Sahib, the Guru's court. There's a story Sikhs love to tell about him. When the Maharaja was once accused of breaking the Sikh code, he was summoned before the Akal Takht and he went, bowed, and accepted its judgment, like any other Sikh. Remember the two flags? The king gave the gold. But the spirit stayed a little higher.
screen: `SUKERCHAKIA MISL, BORN 1780.` · `LAHORE 1799, MAHARAJA 1801.` · `GOLD FOR THE HARMANDIR.` · `A KING WHO BOWED TO THE AKAL TAKHT.` · then, large: `THE GOLDEN TEMPLE.`

segments.voice: Look around you and pick something plain. A mug, a chair, a window, your own hands. Look at it the way pilgrims look at the Golden Temple: slowly, as if it were precious. Where did it come from? Who made it? What has it done for you? Let it shine a little in your attention, without changing anything about it. That's the gold you can add to anything. Then rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Maharaja Ranjit Singh. The Sikh king who united Punjab from 1799, covered the Harmandir in gold, and still bowed to the Akal Takht.
Your line: the golden temple. Today, look at one plain thing as if it were gold. Day two hundred ninety-three.

howItsDone: Sikhs remember Maharaja Ranjit Singh as the ruler of the Sikh Empire; his samadhi stands in Lahore, and the gilding he gave to Harmandir Sahib, which most Sikhs call Darbar Sahib, is renewed and cared for to this day.

original.note: Gurmukhi: Harmandir Sahib, the house of God (Hari); the world calls it the Golden Temple.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Golden Temple was always golden.
what it means: a king's gift of gold to a rebuilt temple, which gave it the name the world knows.

what a scholar hears: the gilding of the upper stories with gilded copper plates was done over years in the early nineteenth century; the story of his summons to the Akal Takht, often linked to Akali Phula Singh, is traditional.

sources.ref: Maharaja Ranjit Singh and the gilding of the Harmandir, as recorded in Sikh history

notes: Taking of Lahore dated July 1799; proclamation as Maharaja 1801 (Vaisakhi); death 1839. Confirm.
Foreign minister Fakir Azizuddin (unnamed in script); confirm.
The Akal Takht summons story (often with Akali Phula Singh and a sentence of flogging later remitted) is traditional; framed as 'a story Sikhs love to tell'.
Exact dates of the gilding (begun about 1802, much of it in the 1830s) are left general.
